Severe Flooding Disrupts Business and Trade Across South Africa

Heavy rains and widespread flooding continue to wreak havoc across South Africa, causing severe disruptions to economic activity and threatening livelihoods in multiple provinces. With the South African Weather Service issuing further warnings, authorities are racing to respond as the crisis deepens.

Since late last week, torrential downpours have battered the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, and Gauteng, with rivers bursting their banks and vital transport links submerged. The Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs confirmed at least 22 fatalities, while thousands have been evacuated from low-lying areas. In Durban, city officials reported that more than 5,000 homes have been damaged or destroyed, leaving residents in urgent need of shelter.

The flooding has had a cascading effect on the economy. Key roads and rail lines connecting Johannesburg, Durban, and Port Elizabeth are impassable, causing major delays in the movement of goods. Sipho Mthembu, spokesperson for the National Road Freight Association, said, “This is the worst transport disruption we’ve seen in years. Deliveries of food, fuel, and medical supplies are severely delayed, impacting businesses and communities nationwide.”

Manufacturing plants in industrial hubs have also been forced to halt operations. The South African Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates that factories in affected regions are operating at less than half capacity, citing power outages and supply chain breakdowns. “Our members are facing unprecedented challenges,” said chamber president Nomvula Dlamini. “Some are unable to access raw materials, while others can’t ship finished products due to road closures and damaged infrastructure.”

Agriculture, a critical sector in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, is also suffering significant losses. Fields of maize and sugarcane have been inundated, and livestock farmers are struggling to safeguard their animals. “We expect crop losses to run into hundreds of millions of rand,” warned Thabo Lekota, chairperson of the Farmers’ Union of South Africa.

Government agencies have deployed emergency teams to the worst-hit areas, but officials acknowledge that relief efforts are hampered by ongoing rains and blocked access routes. President Mthethwa is expected to visit affected communities later this week.

With more rain forecast, analysts warn that the economic toll could mount in the days ahead. “The full impact will only become clear once the floodwaters recede,” said economic analyst Lerato Ndlovu. “But it’s clear that the effects will be felt across the country for months to come.”
